title: Chapter 3 — The Spouter-Inn
paragraphs: Entering that gable-ended Spouter-Inn, you found yourself in a wide, low, straggling entry with old-fashioned wood paneling, reminding you of the bulwarks of some condemned old ship. On one side hung a very large oil painting so thoroughly blackened by smoke, and defaced in every way, that in the uneven crosslights by which you viewed it, it was only by diligent study, a series of systematic visits, and careful inquiry of the neighbors that you could arrive at any understanding of its purpose. There were such unaccountable masses of shades and shadows that at first you almost thought some ambitious young artist, in the time of the New England witches, had tried to depict chaos bewitched. But by dint of much earnest contemplation and oft-repeated pondering, and especially by throwing open the little window toward the back of the entry, you at last came to the conclusion that such an idea, however wild, might not be altogether unwarranted.

But what most puzzled and confounded you was a long, limber, portentous, black mass of something hovering in the center of the picture over three blue, dim, perpendicular lines floating in a nameless yeast. A boggy, soggy, squelchy picture truly, enough to drive a nervous man to distraction. Yet there was a sort of indefinite, half-attained, unimaginable sublimity about it that fairly froze you to it, until you involuntarily swore an oath to yourself to find out what that marvelous painting meant. Every now and then a bright but, alas, deceptive idea would dart through you. — It's the Black Sea in a midnight gale. — It's the unnatural combat of the four primal elements. — It's a blasted heath. — It's a Hyperborean winter scene, from the far frozen north. — It's the breaking-up of the icebound stream of Time. But at last all these fancies yielded to that one portentous something in the middle of the picture. Once that was found out, all the rest would be plain. But wait; doesn't it bear a faint resemblance to a gigantic fish? Even the great leviathan himself?

In fact, the artist's design seemed to be this — a final theory of my own, partly based on the combined opinions of many old people I talked with on the subject. The picture shows a Cape-Horner — a ship rounding Cape Horn — in a great hurricane; the half-foundered ship is wallowing there with only its three dismantled masts visible; and an exasperated whale, intending to spring clean over the vessel, is in the enormous act of impaling himself on the three mastheads.

The opposite wall of this entry was hung all over with a heathenish array of monstrous clubs and spears. Some were thickly set with glittering teeth resembling ivory saws; others were tufted with knots of human hair; and one was sickle-shaped, with a vast handle sweeping around like the curve a long-armed mower cuts in new-mown grass. You shuddered as you gazed, and wondered what monstrous cannibal and savage could ever have gone death-harvesting with such a hacking, horrifying implement. Mixed with these were rusty old whaling lances and harpoons, all broken and deformed. Some were storied weapons. With this once-long lance, now wildly bent at the elbow, Nathan Swain killed fifteen whales between one sunrise and sunset fifty years ago. And that harpoon — so like a corkscrew now — was thrown in Javan seas, and run away with by a whale that was killed years afterward off the Cape of Blanco. The original iron entered near the tail and, like a restless needle wandering around in the body of a man, traveled a full forty feet, and at last was found embedded in the hump.

Crossing this dusky entry, and going on through that low-arched way — cut through what in old times must have been a great central chimney with fireplaces all around — you enter the public room. This is an even duskier place, with such low, ponderous beams above and such old wrinkled planks beneath that you would almost imagine you were treading some old ship's cockpits, especially on such a howling night, when this corner-anchored old ark rocked so furiously. On one side stood a long, low, shelf-like table covered with cracked glass cases, filled with dusty rarities gathered from the remotest nooks of this wide world. Projecting from the farther corner of the room stands a dark-looking den — the bar — a crude attempt at a right whale's head. Be that as it may, there stands the vast arched bone of the whale's jaw, so wide that a coach might almost drive beneath it. Inside are shabby shelves lined with old decanters, bottles, and flasks; and in those jaws of swift destruction, like another cursed Jonah (which indeed is what they called him), bustles a little withered old man who, for their money, sells the sailors delirium and death at a dear price.

Abominable are the tumblers into which he pours his poison. Though they were true cylinders outside, inside, the villainous green goggling glasses tapered deceitfully downward to a cheating bottom. Parallel meridians, crudely pecked into the glass, circle these robbers' goblets. Fill to this mark, and your charge is only a penny; to this one, a penny more; and so on up to the full glass — the Cape Horn measure, which you may gulp down for a shilling.

When I entered the place I found a number of young seamen gathered around a table, examining by a dim light various specimens of skrimshander — sailors' carved bone and ivory work. I looked for the landlord, and when I told him I wanted a room, he answered that his house was full — not a bed unoccupied. "But hold on," he added, tapping his forehead, "you ain't got no objections to sharing a harpooner's blanket, have you? I s'pose you're goin' whaling, so you'd better get used to that sort of thing."

I told him I never liked sleeping two to a bed; that if I ever did, it would depend on who the harpooner turned out to be; and that if he (the landlord) really had nowhere else to put me, and the harpooner wasn't downright objectionable, then rather than wander any farther around a strange town on such a bitter night, I would settle for half of any decent man's blanket.
"Thought so. All right, have a seat. Supper? You want supper? Supper'll be ready directly."

I sat down on an old wooden bench carved all over like a seat on the Battery. At one end, a ruminative sailor was further decorating it with his jackknife, stooping over and working diligently at the space between his knees. He was attempting a ship under full sail, but he wasn't making much headway, I thought.

At last some four or five of us were summoned to our meal in an adjoining room. It was cold as Iceland — no fire at all; the landlord said he couldn't afford it. Nothing but two dismal tallow candles, each wrapped in a winding sheet of dripped tallow. We had to button up our monkey jackets and hold cups of scalding tea to our lips with our half-frozen fingers. But the food was of the most substantial kind — not only meat and potatoes, but dumplings; good heavens! Dumplings for supper! One young fellow in a green box coat went at these dumplings in a most alarming manner.
"My boy," said the landlord, "you'll have nightmares to a dead certainty."
"Landlord," I whispered, "that ain't the harpooner, is it?"
"Oh, no," he said, looking sort of diabolically funny, "the harpooner is a dark-complexioned chap. He never eats dumplings, he don't — he eats nothing but steaks, and he likes 'em rare."
"The devil he does," I said. "Where is that harpooner? Is he here?"
"He'll be here before long," was the answer.

I couldn't help it: I started to feel suspicious of this "dark-complexioned" harpooner. At any rate, I decided that if it turned out we really had to share a bed, he would have to undress and get in before I did.
After supper, the company returned to the bar room. Having nothing else to do, I decided to spend the rest of the evening as a spectator.

Soon a riotous noise was heard outside. Jumping up, the landlord cried, "That's the Grampus's crew. I seen her reported in the offing this morning — a three years' voyage, and a full ship. Hurrah, boys; now we'll have the latest news from the Fijis."

We heard sea boots tramping in the entry; the door was flung open, and in rolled a wild enough bunch of sailors. Bundled in shaggy watch coats, their heads wrapped in woolen scarves darned all over and ragged, and their beards stiff with icicles, they looked like a horde of bears erupting out of Labrador. They had just come ashore from their boat, and this was the first house they had walked into. No wonder, then, that they steered straight for the whale's mouth — the bar — where the wrinkled little old Jonah on duty soon poured them all brimming glasses. One of them complained of a bad head cold, so Jonah mixed him a potion like pitch, of gin and molasses, which he swore was a sure cure for any cold or catarrh whatever, no matter how long you'd had it, or whether you'd caught it off the coast of Labrador or on the windward side of an ice island.
The liquor quickly went to their heads, as it usually does with even the heaviest drinkers who've just come ashore, and they began leaping about wildly.

I noticed, however, that one of them held somewhat apart, and though he seemed anxious not to spoil his shipmates' hilarity with his own sober face, on the whole he refrained from making as much noise as the rest. This man interested me at once; and since the sea-gods had ordained that he should soon become my shipmate (though only a sleeping-partner one, as far as this narrative is concerned), I will venture a little description of him here. He stood a full six feet tall, with noble shoulders and a chest like a coffer-dam. I have seldom seen such brawn in a man. His face was deeply browned and sunburnt, which made his white teeth dazzling by contrast; while in the deep shadows of his eyes floated some memories that did not seem to give him much joy. His voice at once announced that he was a Southerner, and from his fine stature I thought he must be one of those tall mountaineers from the Alleghanian Ridge in Virginia. When the revelry of his companions had reached its height, this man slipped away unobserved, and I saw no more of him until he became my comrade on the sea. Within a few minutes, however, his shipmates missed him, and since he was, it seems, for some reason a huge favorite with them, they raised a cry of "Bulkington! Bulkington! Where's Bulkington?" and dashed out of the house after him.

It was now about nine o'clock. The room felt almost supernaturally quiet after all that carousing, and I began congratulating myself on a little plan that had occurred to me just before the sailors arrived.

Nobody actually prefers sleeping two in a bed. In fact, you'd much rather not share one even with your own brother. I don't know why, but people like privacy when they sleep. And when it comes to sleeping beside a stranger you don't know, in a strange inn, in a strange town — and that stranger a harpooner — your objections multiply without end. Nor was there any earthly reason why I, as a sailor, should share a bed any more than anyone else; sailors at sea no more sleep two in a bed than bachelor kings do on land. True, they all sleep together in one room, but you have your own hammock, you cover yourself with your own blanket, and you sleep in your own skin.

The more I pondered this harpooner, the more I loathed the thought of sleeping with him. It was fair to assume that, being a harpooner, his linen or woolens, as the case might be, would not be of the tidiest, and certainly not of the finest. I began to twitch all over. Besides, it was getting late, and my decent harpooner ought to be home and heading for bed. Suppose, now, he should tumble in on me at midnight — how could I tell what vile hole he had been coming from?
"Landlord! I've changed my mind about that harpooner. I won't sleep with him. I'll try the bench here."

"Just as you please. I'm sorry I can't spare you a tablecloth for a mattress, and it's a plaguy rough board here" — feeling the knots and notches. "But wait a bit, Skrimshander; I've got a carpenter's plane there in the bar — wait, I say, and I'll make you snug enough." So saying, he fetched the plane, first dusted the bench with his old silk handkerchief, and set to vigorously planing away at my bed, grinning like an ape all the while. The shavings flew right and left, until at last the plane blade came bump against an indestructible knot. The landlord nearly sprained his wrist, and I told him for heaven's sake to quit — the bed was soft enough to suit me, and I didn't know how all the planing in the world could make eiderdown out of a pine plank. So, gathering up the shavings with another grin and throwing them into the great stove in the middle of the room, he went about his business and left me lost in a brown study.

Next I measured the bench and found it was a foot too short, though a chair could fix that. But it was also a foot too narrow, and the other bench in the room stood about four inches higher than the planed one, so there was no hitching the two together. Then I set the first bench lengthwise along the only clear stretch of wall, leaving a small gap between for my back to settle into. But I soon discovered that such a cold draft blew over me from under the windowsill that this plan was no good at all — especially since another current coming from the rickety door met the one from the window, and the two of them together whipped up a series of little whirlwinds right around the spot where I had meant to spend the night.

The devil take that harpooner, I thought. But wait — couldn't I steal a march on him: bolt his door on the inside and jump into his bed, not to be woken by the most violent knocking? It seemed no bad idea; but on second thought I dismissed it. For who could tell but that the next morning, as soon as I popped out of the room, the harpooner might be standing in the entry, all ready to knock me down!

Still, looking around me again and seeing no possible chance of spending a bearable night except in some other person's bed, I began to think that I might, after all, be harboring unwarranted prejudices against this unknown harpooner. I'll wait a while, I thought; he must be dropping in before long. I'll have a good look at him then, and perhaps we may become jolly good bedfellows after all — there's no telling.
But though the other boarders kept coming in by ones, twos, and threes and going to bed, there was still no sign of my harpooner.
"Landlord!" I said. "What sort of fellow is he — does he always keep such late hours?" It was now close to twelve o'clock.

The landlord chuckled again with his lean chuckle, and seemed mightily tickled at something beyond my comprehension. "No," he answered, "generally he's an early bird — early to bed and early to rise — yes, he's the bird what catches the worm. But tonight he went out a-peddling, you see, and I don't see what on earth keeps him so late, unless, maybe, he can't sell his head."

"Can't sell his head? What sort of a bamboozling story is this you're telling me?" I said, getting into a towering rage. "Do you mean to say, landlord, that this harpooner is actually busy this blessed Saturday night, or rather Sunday morning, peddling his head around this town?"
"That's exactly it," said the landlord, "and I told him he couldn't sell it here. The market's overstocked."
"Overstocked with what?" I shouted.
"With heads, of course. Aren't there too many heads in the world?"
"Look here, landlord," I said, quite calmly, "you'd better stop spinning that yarn to me. I'm not green."
"Maybe not," he said, taking out a stick and whittling a toothpick, "but I rather guess you'll be done brown if that there harpooner hears you a-slanderin' his head."
"I'll break it for him," I said, now flying into a rage again at the landlord's incomprehensible nonsense.
"It's broke already," he said.
"Broke?" I said. "Broke, do you mean?"
"Sartain, and that's the very reason he can't sell it, I guess."

"Landlord," I said, going up to him as cool as Iceland's volcano Mount Hekla in a snowstorm — "landlord, stop whittling. You and I must understand one another, and without delay, too. I come to your house and want a bed; you tell me you can only give me half of one; that the other half belongs to a certain harpooner. And about this harpooner, whom I have not yet seen, you persist in telling me the most mystifying and exasperating stories, which tend to give me an uncomfortable feeling toward the man you intend for my bedfellow — a sort of connection, landlord, which is an intimate and confidential one in the highest degree. I now demand that you speak out and tell me who and what this harpooner is, and whether I shall be safe in every respect spending the night with him. And in the first place, you will be so good as to take back that story about selling his head, which, if true, I take to be good evidence that this harpooner is stark mad; and I've no idea of sleeping with a madman; and you, sir — you, I mean, landlord — you, sir, by trying to get me to do so knowingly, would thereby make yourself liable to criminal prosecution."

"Well," said the landlord, fetching a long breath, "that's a purty long sermon for a chap that swears a little now and then. But be easy, be easy — this here harpooner I been tellin' you of has just arrived from the South Seas, where he bought up a lot of 'balmed New Zealand heads (great curios, you know), and he's sold all of 'em but one, and that one he's trying to sell tonight, 'cause tomorrow's Sunday, and it wouldn't do to be sellin' human heads about the streets when folks is goin' to church. He wanted to, last Sunday, but I stopped him just as he was goin' out the door with four heads strung on a string, for all the world like a string of onions."

This explanation cleared up what would otherwise have been an unaccountable mystery, and showed that the landlord hadn't meant to fool me after all. But at the same time, what was I to think of a harpooner who stayed out on a Saturday night straight through into the holy Sabbath, doing such cannibal business as selling dead idolaters' heads?
"Depend on it, landlord, that harpooner is a dangerous man."

"He pays reg'lar," was the reply. "But come, it's getting dreadful late; you'd better be turning flukes — turning in. It's a nice bed; Sal and me slept in that there bed the night we were spliced. There's plenty of room for two to kick about in that bed; it's an almighty big bed, that. Why, before we gave it up, Sal used to put our Sam and little Johnny in the foot of it. But I got to dreaming and sprawling about one night, and somehow Sam got pitched on the floor and came near breaking his arm. After that, Sal said it wouldn't do. Come along here, I'll give you a light in a jiffy." And so saying, he lit a candle and held it toward me, offering to lead the way. But I stood undecided; when, looking at a clock in the corner, he exclaimed, "I vow, it's Sunday — you won't see that harpooner tonight; he's come to anchor somewhere. Come along, then; do come; won't you come?"

I considered the matter a moment, and then up the stairs we went, and I was shown into a small room, cold as a clam, and furnished, sure enough, with a prodigious bed, almost big enough, in fact, for any four harpooners to sleep side by side.

"There," said the landlord, setting the candle on a crazy old sea chest that did double duty as a washstand and center table. "There, make yourself comfortable now, and good night to you." I turned around from eyeing the bed, but he had disappeared.

Folding back the counterpane, I bent over the bed. Though not the most elegant, it stood up to inspection tolerably well. I then glanced around the room; and besides the bedstead and the center table, I could see no other furniture belonging to the place but a crude shelf, the four walls, and a papered fireboard showing a man striking a whale. Of things not properly belonging to the room, there was a hammock lashed up and thrown on the floor in one corner; also a large seaman's bag, containing the harpooner's wardrobe, no doubt, in place of a land trunk. There was also a bundle of outlandish bone fishhooks on the shelf over the fireplace, and a tall harpoon standing at the head of the bed.

But what's this on the chest? I picked it up, held it near the light, felt it, sniffed it, and tried every way I could think of to reach some satisfying conclusion about it. The only thing I can compare it to is a big doormat, trimmed around the edges with little tinkling tags rather like the dyed porcupine quills on an Indian moccasin. There was a hole or slit in the middle of this mat, the kind you see in South American ponchos. But could any sober harpooner really climb into a doormat and parade through the streets of a Christian town dressed like that? I put it on to try it, and it dragged me down like a hamper, being unusually shaggy and thick, and, I thought, slightly damp, as if this mysterious harpooner had worn it on a rainy day. Wearing it, I went over to a scrap of mirror stuck on the wall, and I never saw such a sight in my life. I pulled myself out of it in such a rush that I gave myself a crick in the neck.

I sat on the edge of the bed and started thinking about this head-peddling harpooner and his doormat. After thinking a while there on the bedside, I got up, took off my monkey jacket, and stood in the middle of the room, thinking. Then I took off my coat and thought some more in my shirtsleeves. But I was beginning to feel very cold, half undressed as I was, and I remembered the landlord saying the harpooner wouldn't be coming home at all that night, since it was so very late; so without any more fuss I jumped out of my trousers and boots, blew out the light, tumbled into bed, and committed myself to heaven's care.

Whether that mattress was stuffed with corncobs or broken dishes, I can't say, but I tossed and turned a good deal and lay awake for a long time. At last I drifted into a light doze, and had very nearly made a good offing toward the land of Nod, when I heard a heavy tread in the passage and saw a glimmer of light come into the room under the door.

Lord save me, I thought, that must be the harpooner, the infernal head-peddler. But I lay perfectly still, and resolved not to say a word until spoken to. Holding a light in one hand, and that same New Zealand head in the other, the stranger entered the room and, without looking toward the bed, placed his candle a good way off from me on the floor in one corner, and then began working away at the knotted cords of the large bag I mentioned before as being in the room. I was all eagerness to see his face, but he kept it turned away for some time while busy unlacing the bag's mouth. This done, however, he turned around — when, good heavens! What a sight! Such a face! It was of a dark, purplish, yellow color, stuck over here and there with large blackish-looking squares. Yes, it's just as I thought: he's a terrible bedfellow; he's been in a fight, got dreadfully cut, and here he is, just back from the surgeon. But at that moment he happened to turn his face toward the light in such a way that I plainly saw those black squares on his cheeks could not be sticking-plasters at all. They were stains of some sort or other. At first I didn't know what to make of this; but soon an inkling of the truth occurred to me. I remembered a story of a white man — a whaleman, too — who, falling among the cannibals, had been tattooed by them. I concluded that this harpooner, in the course of his distant voyages, must have met with a similar adventure. And what is it, after all, I thought! It's only his outside; a man can be honest in any sort of skin. But then, what to make of his unearthly complexion — the part of it, I mean, lying round about, and completely independent of, the squares of tattooing? To be sure, it might be nothing but a good coat of tropical tanning; but I never heard of a hot sun tanning a white man into a purplish yellow one. However, I had never been in the South Seas; and perhaps the sun there produced these extraordinary effects on the skin. Now, while all these ideas were passing through me like lightning, this harpooner never noticed me at all. But after some difficulty in opening his bag, he began fumbling in it, and soon pulled out a sort of tomahawk and a sealskin wallet with the hair still on. Placing these on the old chest in the middle of the room, he then took the New Zealand head — a ghastly enough thing — and crammed it down into the bag. He now took off his hat — a new beaver hat — when I came near crying out with fresh surprise. There was no hair on his head — none to speak of, at least — nothing but a small scalp-knot twisted up on his forehead. His bald purplish head now looked for all the world like a mildewed skull. If the stranger had not stood between me and the door, I would have bolted out of it quicker than I ever bolted a dinner.

Even so, I half thought of slipping out through the window, but this was the second floor, at the back. I'm no coward, but what to make of this head-peddling purple rascal was completely beyond me. Ignorance is the parent of fear, and since I was utterly baffled and bewildered by the stranger, I admit I was now as frightened of him as if the devil himself had broken into my room like this in the dead of night. In fact, I was so scared of him that just then I didn't have the nerve to speak to him and demand a satisfactory explanation of what seemed so inexplicable about him.

Meanwhile he kept on undressing, and at last uncovered his chest and arms. As I live, those hidden parts of him were checkered with the same squares as his face; his back was covered in the same dark squares too; he looked as if he had fought in a Thirty Years' War and just escaped with a shirt of sticking plaster. What's more, even his legs were marked, as if a crowd of dark green frogs were running up the trunks of young palm trees. It was now perfectly clear that he must be some abominable savage or other who had signed onto a whaler in the South Seas and so ended up in this Christian country. I shook at the thought. A head-peddler, too — maybe the heads of his own brothers. He might take a liking to mine — heavens! Look at that tomahawk!

But there was no time for shuddering, because the savage now started on something that absolutely riveted my attention and convinced me he really must be a heathen. He went to his heavy grego, or wrap-all, or dreadnaught — a thick sea coat — which he had hung on a chair earlier, rummaged in the pockets, and finally brought out a strange little misshapen figure with a hump on its back, exactly the color of a three-day-old Congo baby. Remembering the embalmed head, I nearly thought at first that this black manikin was a real baby preserved in some similar way. But seeing that it wasn't flexible at all, and that it gleamed a lot like polished ebony, I decided it must be just a wooden idol, which is exactly what it turned out to be. For now the savage goes over to the empty fireplace, takes away the papered fire-board, and sets this little hunchbacked figure up between the andirons like a bowling pin. The sides of the chimney and all the bricks inside were thick with soot, so I thought this fireplace made a very fitting little shrine or chapel for his Congo idol.

I now squinted hard toward the half-hidden image, feeling quite uneasy all the while, to see what would come next. First he takes about two handfuls of wood shavings out of his grego pocket and lays them carefully in front of the idol; then he puts a piece of ship's biscuit on top, holds the lamp flame to it, and lights the shavings into a sacrificial blaze. After a while, following many quick grabs into the fire and even quicker retreats of his fingers (which he seemed to be burning badly), he finally managed to pull the biscuit out; then, blowing off a bit of the heat and ash, he politely offered it to the little negro. But the little devil didn't seem to care for such dry fare at all; he never moved his lips. All these strange antics came with even stranger throaty noises from the worshipper, who seemed to be praying in a singsong, or else singing some pagan psalm or other, while his face twitched in the most unnatural way. At last he put out the fire, picked up the idol without any ceremony, and bagged it in his grego pocket again as casually as a hunter bagging a dead woodcock.

All these strange doings made me increasingly uncomfortable. Seeing that he was now showing every sign of concluding his business operations and jumping into bed with me, I decided it was high time — now or never, before the light was put out — to break the spell I'd been under for so long.

But the moment I spent working out what to say proved fatal. He picked up his tomahawk from the table, looked at its head for an instant, and then, holding it to the light with his mouth on the handle, puffed out great clouds of tobacco smoke. The next moment the light went out, and this wild cannibal, tomahawk between his teeth, leaped into bed with me. I shouted — I couldn't help it now — and with a sudden grunt of astonishment he began feeling me.

Stammering out something, I don't know what, I rolled away from him against the wall, and then begged him, whoever or whatever he might be, to keep quiet and let me get up and light the lamp again. But his guttural replies convinced me at once that he only poorly understood what I meant.
"Who-e debel you?" he said at last. "You no speak-e, dam-me, I kill-e." And so saying, he began flourishing the lighted tomahawk about me in the dark.
"Landlord, for God's sake! Peter Coffin!" I shouted. "Landlord! Watchman! Coffin! Angels! Save me!"

"Speak-e! Tell-ee me who-ee be, or dam-me, I kill-e!" the cannibal growled again, while his horrid flourishings of the tomahawk scattered the hot tobacco ashes about me until I thought my shirt would catch fire. But thank heaven, at that moment the landlord came into the room, light in hand, and leaping from the bed I ran up to him.
"Don't be afraid now," he said, grinning again. "Queequeg here wouldn't harm a hair of your head."
"Stop your grinning," I shouted, "and why didn't you tell me that that infernal harpooner was a cannibal?"

"I thought you knowed it — didn't I tell you he was a-peddlin' heads around town? But turn flukes again and go to sleep. Queequeg, look here — you sabbee me, I sabbee — you this man sleepe you — you sabbee?"
"Me sabbee plenty," grunted Queequeg, puffing away at his pipe and sitting up in bed.

"You gettee in," he added, motioning to me with his tomahawk and throwing the bedclothes to one side. He really did this in not only a civil but a truly kind and charitable way. I stood looking at him a moment. For all his tattooing, he was on the whole a clean, comely-looking cannibal. What's all this fuss I've been making about? I thought to myself. The man's a human being just as I am; he has just as much reason to fear me as I have to be afraid of him. Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian.

"Landlord," I said, "tell him to stash his tomahawk there, or pipe, or whatever you call it — tell him to stop smoking, in short, and I'll turn in with him. But I don't fancy having a man smoking in bed with me. It's dangerous. Besides, I ain't insured."
When this was told to Queequeg, he at once complied, and again politely motioned me to get into bed — rolling over to one side as much as to say, "I won't touch a leg of you."
"Good night, landlord," I said. "You may go."
I turned in, and never slept better in my life.
